analysis.one_liner: Makes straw-purchasing and gun trafficking federal crimes with stiff prison terms.
analysis.headline: A bill to punish firearms trafficking, introduced after the shooting death of a Chicago teenager, never received a committee vote or floor action in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime to buy a gun for someone who cannot legally own one (a "straw purchase"), and to knowingly move two or more guns to someone who will use them illegally. It sets prison terms of 15 years, rising to 25 years for large trafficking operations or guns meant for violent crimes, adds gun trafficking to the crimes that allow court-ordered wiretaps and racketeering and money-laundering charges, requires forfeiture of trafficking profits, and directs the Sentencing Commission to raise penalties for traffickers tied to gangs or cartels.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities hit by illegal gun violence — particularly in cities like Chicago, where trafficked guns are a leading source of crime weapons. The bill is named for Hadiya Pendleton, a Chicago teenager shot in a park in 2013, and Nyasia Pryear-Yard, a New Jersey teenager killed in 2009.
analysis.who_benefits_short: City neighborhoods plagued by illegal guns

how_it_helps.text: Creates new federal crimes for straw purchasing (buying a gun for someone else) and for trafficking two or more guns, with prison terms up to 15 years and up to 25 years when guns are destined for violent crimes or a five-person ring is involved [S2][S3].

Adds these offenses to the crimes for which wiretaps may be authorized, and to racketeering and money-laundering definitions, letting prosecutors build cases against trafficking networks the way they do against drug organizations [S3].
Requires forfeiture of property and proceeds from trafficking convictions and doubles the maximum fine to twice the trafficking profits, hitting the money behind the trade [S2][S3].
Directs the Sentencing Commission to raise guideline penalties for straw purchases and trafficking, with higher penalties for offenders tied to gangs, cartels, or organized crime [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms traffickers, straw purchasers, and gun sellers who knowingly sell to disqualified buyers face much longer prison terms and asset forfeiture. Licensed gun dealers could face more federal scrutiny of the sales at their counters, since most trafficked guns start as a legal-looking purchase.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun traffickers and dealers who look the other way

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on longer prison sentences, wiretaps, and mandatory forfeiture — heavy law-enforcement tools whose deterrent effect is debated, and which raise civil-liberties concerns about surveillance and prosecutorial power [S3].

The mental-state standard is 'reasonable cause to believe' rather than actual knowledge, meaning a person could face up to 15 years for buying a gun as a gift for someone they had reason to suspect was disqualified, even if they did not know it [S3].

Longer federal sentences fall most heavily on low-level participants — the friend or girlfriend who carries out the straw purchase — while ringleaders' penalties depend on prosecutors choosing to use the enhancement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks the supply chain of illegal guns — the straw purchase at the counter and the trunk-load transported across state lines — rather than lawful ownership, and it preserves explicit exceptions for bona fide gifts and raffle winners. The trade-off is that it expands federal surveillance and adds more lengthy mandatory-adjacent sentencing on top of an already punitive federal code, and heavier sentences alone do not shut down the trade if enforcement stays thin.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary Committee, then in its crime subcommittee, and the Congress ended in January 2015 with no markup, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 5, 2013 by Rep. Bobby Rush of Illinois and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1][S5].
On April 8, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security and Investigations, where it stayed [S5].
It gathered 14 cosponsors, all Democrats, and the House never took a recorded vote on it before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms traffickers and the secondary-market sellers who supply them are better off, because the rules that would have exposed their trade to racketeering, wiretap, and forfeiture tools were never enacted. Gun-rights advocates opposed to expanding federal firearms crimes also kept the status quo.

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it for Hadiya Pendleton, a Chicago teenager shot dead in a park in 2013.

for.name: 14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 14 were Democrats.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill; it remained in the crime subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Brought no firearms-related bills of this kind to the floor in 2013, a period of intense fight over gun legislation after the Sandy Hook shooting.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; with Republicans holding the House majority and the Judiciary chair, the bill never advanced, and no roll-call vote was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Firearms traffickers and the illegal secondary market
industries.note: The bill's core target: buyers-for-others and movers of multiple guns would face 15-to-25-year terms, wiretaps, racketeering charges, and loss of profits and property. These are the actors whose supply of guns to criminals drives urban gun violence.

Dealers are exempted from the new straw-purchase crime themselves, but the law criminalizes the purchases made at their counters on behalf of disqualified buyers, which would push them toward refusing suspect sales. The industry consistently fought legislation expanding liability and enforcement around retail gun sales, and this bill stalled without any of it taking effect.
